entry.title: La sincerità? Santa Maradona, still a generation’s portrait twenty-five years on

link.title: La sincerità? Santa Maradona, still a generation’s portrait twenty-five years on

entry.content:
I had just finished my bachelor’s in Mathematics and was about to start a master’s in Economics. In between, I had an interview with a consulting firm, for a position in the software development unit.

During the interview came the inevitable question: your greatest strength, your worst weakness. I answered la sincerità, sincerity, both times.

I had always wanted to quote Santa Maradona in an interview, and that day, strangely enough, I did. But first, the film.

The film

Santa Maradona is a film by Marco Ponti, released in 2001. It is set among disillusioned young graduates in Turin, a generation that keeps missing the target, then as now. It follows Andrea (Stefano Accorsi), who drifts from one job interview to the next. Bart (Libero De Rienzo), his flatmate, calls himself a literary critic: a cousin in Sicily emails him reviews from a local paper, and Bart signs and sends them on without reading either the book or the review. They share a flat, and before long being precarious becomes almost something to boast about:

Andrea: The rent is off the books. We don’t work, we’re not on any unemployment register… technically, we don’t exist!
Bart: I’d say it with a bit less pride, though.

The film opens with one of Andrea’s interviews:

Employer: What would you say is your greatest strength?
Andrea: Sincerity.
Employer: And your main weakness?
Andrea: Sincerity.
Employer: What is your highest aspiration?
Andrea: Sincerity.
Employer: You’re a sharp young man, I see. So tell me: what is your family’s annual income?
Andrea: Sincerity?

A hundred times

I first saw it in high school, in bits and pieces, on the tiny screen of an iPod video. I must have watched it a hundred times since, and I know the lines by heart.

One of my favourite scenes is in a bookshop. Bart is explaining that he can’t stand books because they’re too expensive, when a customer, who has mistaken him for a shop assistant, asks him for help. She has mixed up two titles that, in Italian, sound almost the same: Stefano Benni’s La compagnia dei celestini and James Redfield’s The Celestine Prophecy (La profezia di Celestino):

Well, madam, I’m afraid there’s a slight confusion about the title. So, you’re confusing La compagnia dei celestini, Stefano Benni, Feltrinelli, with La profezia di Celestino, James Redfield, Corbaccio? Corbaccio. Calm down, excuse me a moment, please. You should know that James Redfield’s book, La profezia di Celestino, is a crappy little new age book, and we don’t stock crappy little new age books here. Did you hear my colleague? Whereas La compagnia dei celestini is a bestseller, and we don’t stock bestsellers here, we only have quality books. Is that clear? There you go, thank you, madam, make yourself comfortable, that’s the door.

But the scene almost everyone remembers is the run. It’s a game among friends. Dolores, one of the group, is wearing a wedding dress; she pretends that Andrea only wants to marry her because she’s pregnant, and runs off in tears. The others chase after her to bring her back, and instead they just run, laughing, through the ground-level fountains of Piazza Castello.

For anyone who grew up in Turin, that square means something specific: on the last day of high school, we all met there, whatever school we came from, for water fights. Watching that run takes me back there.

Australia

Throughout the film, Andrea’s safety net is a job in his uncle’s family business, which sells shower cubicles: the emblem of settling for less. In the final scene, Andrea and Bart are watching Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid on TV:

Andrea: What if it really is too late?
Bart: What do you think?
Andrea: I don’t know. Let’s turn everything off and get far away from here.
Bart: And go where?
Butch Cassidy (on TV): Australia.
Andrea: Australia.
Bart: Australia?
Andrea: Yes, Australia.
Bart: Australia’s no better than here, Butch.
Andrea: Australia, Sundance. Endless places to hide. Good weather, good sea… think about it.
Bart: All right, I’ll think about it.
[…]
Bart: And now? Shower cubicle?
Andrea: No. Now let’s try to fix things.

My partner and I always say “Australia” whenever we plan our future, elsewhere, anywhere, together. The film means a lot to us. Our first purchase as a couple was a reproduction of the original script, with the shooting notes and stills. It was a limited edition, and the proceeds went to the Candiolo cancer research centre.1

The target

In the end, they offered me a position, in Milan or in Turin. I turned it down. Not because I didn’t like programming: I liked it then and I still do, and programming languages have always fascinated me. But after years of mathematics I wasn’t ready to stop studying. The master’s took me down another road: to the PhD, to research, to my partner, and to where I am now and the people I share it with.

Today, a quarter of a century after the film came out, I’m on the academic job market. This time, the job I’m looking for is the one I chose back then, by turning down the other.

Santa Maradona is the portrait of a generation that kept missing the target: interviews that went nowhere, CVs nobody answered, irony as a shield. Some things haven’t changed: most contracts have an end date, mine included. But I have a partner I love and who loves me, a daughter who isn’t mine by blood but is in every other way, and another one due in January. And I’m enjoying every bit of it. When I think of my family, I believe I hit the target.

And if someone asked me today about my strengths and weaknesses, I would still answer la sincerità.

TL;DR?

I quoted Santa Maradona in a job interview, and then turned that job down.
I hit the target once. Whatever comes next, I’m still aiming.

entry.summary: What do you answer when asked for your greatest strength and your worst weakness? A cult Italian film from 2001, a run through a square in Turin, and the target I believe I hit.

entry.title: My heart is here
entry.content:
It all started with a drawing.

She was about four, and I had something hard to explain: that even when I have to leave, my heart stays there, with her and her mom. And lately, with the little sister on the way, too.

The trouble is that, for a child, time doesn’t work the way it does for us. “Tomorrow” and “in five days” are the same vague amount of time. And so is “yesterday.”

Can we play like yesterday, when you pretended to fall?

That “yesterday,” almost innocent, meant three months earlier.

The drawing, though, worked. She usually takes drawings down after a few days. This one has been on the wall, in the same spot, for over a year, and she has never touched it.

So I thought: if time can’t be explained, maybe it can be shown. And instead of buying a paper calendar, I coded one.

It’s called Magic Calendar, it’s a desktop app for Mac and Windows, and it’s free.

We’re here, my heart is here

The heart of the app, literally, is two kinds of day:

  • “We’re here!”: the days we’re together;
  • “My heart is here”: the days I’m away, but my heart stays with them.

Two colors, two emoji, and a kind of time that can finally be counted: the little squares left until the next “We’re here!”

Then the thing happened that always happens to projects started for fun: someone began using it for real. A friend with two five-year-olds uses it to keep track of their weekly activities. And a calendar made for one little girl became a calendar for families.

What it does (in short)

For those who just want to know if they need it

  • Monthly and weekly views, with themes, emoji, and your own images.
  • Day types you invent: together, away, school, grandparents, whatever you need.
  • School days and holidays in different colors, long weekends, and your town’s patron saint’s day. And now you can import the school calendar straight from an .ics file, if your school publishes one.
  • Select several days at once and set repeating patterns (every other week, too), with Undo for when you get carried away.
  • A countdown to the next day of each type. (Yes, it’s the most important feature of all.)
  • PDF export, to print and stick on the fridge, and export to Apple Calendar or Google Calendar.
  • Everything stays on your computer: no accounts, no servers, no data collected.

A spaceship in outer space

This isn’t the first time my work has crossed paths with children.

With MinUTo, a University of Bologna project on mindful parenting, I ran online experiments with children. We pretended to be on a spaceship in outer space. I watched them fly off on their imagination, be patient (or not), push their luck, and be disappointed.

I watched painfully shy kids change in less than forty minutes: trust, open up. And I met kids so excited that they gave me little gifts, or a drawing.

Later, I also worked on the rollout of the MinUTo web app1, bringing it to schools and families.

What stayed with me is this: with children, what works is what they can see, touch, and count. Magic Calendar, in its small way, comes from the same idea.

What I learned

  • “Just for fun” is the most dangerous phrase in software. From 1.0 to 1.7 is a short trip, and every version came with its own request: “what if I could mark school days too?”, “what if I could print it?”
  • Automatic updates beat any feature. Nobody goes to GitHub to download a new version on their own. Now the app updates itself: you publish, it replaces itself.

Where to get it

The app is on GitHub: just download the latest version for your computer. It’s free for personal and educational use.

If you use it and find a bug, open an issue on GitHub or leave a comment below. And if you use it and don’t find any bugs, write anyway: that doesn’t happen often.

TL;DR?

For a child, “tomorrow” and “three months from now” are the same thing.
A calendar doesn’t make the wait shorter, but it makes it visible. And once you can see it, it’s less scary.

  1. The app is available in Italian, English, and French. ↩︎
entry.summary: How Magic Calendar came to be: a family calendar that started with a drawing and a simple idea. For a child, “tomorrow” and “in five days” are the same distance away.

entry.title: How formal should an email be?

link.title: How formal should an email be?

entry.content:
Every professor has received this email:

Can you tell me where the exam is held?

(Spoiler: most universities have a dedicated page with this information, updated with near-religious devotion. And if that’s not enough, there’s the student office. Worth a look before writing.)

Every year, thousands of students email their professors. And very often—not out of malice, but out of inexperience—the result is a small communicative disaster: awkward greetings, insurance-contract phrasing, missing punctuation.

So, taking inspiration from “Poche semplici regole per scrivere una e-mail ad un professore” (A few simple rules for writing an email to a professor) by Professor Davide Dragone, here’s my personal take on how to write good emails to faculty. Because between overly formal wording, impersonal verbs, and the panic of not remembering whether the professor told me to use their first name… I’ve struggled too.

Let’s start with some real examples—from ultra-formal to… yikes.

Sample emails (from most formal to… let’s say “less ideal”)

1. The perfectly formal one

For those aiming to impress either the Academy or the Royal Family

Subject: Econometrics: slides for lecture 10
Dear Professor Lecter,
My name is C-3PO, and I am enrolled in your Econometrics course.
I am writing to ask whether the slides for lecture 10 will be made available online.
Thank you in advance for your time.
Best regards,
C-3PO

  • Pros: flawless, clear, professional.
  • Cons: could’ve been written by a highly educated chatbot.
  • Reader’s reaction: approval… mixed with slight existential boredom.

2. The balanced approach

Human, polite, effective—my favorite

Subject: Econometrics: slides for lecture 10
Dear Professor Lecter,
I’m C-3PO, a student in your Econometrics course. I was wondering if the slides for lecture 10 will be uploaded to the course page soon.
Thanks in advance, and have a great day!
C-3PO

  • Pros: direct, respectful, perfect in most cases.
  • Cons: none. Save it as a draft and reuse forever.
  • Reader’s reaction: smile, fast reply, instant respect.

3. The “yeah, fine” email

Casual but respectful. Aka: normal.

Hi Professor,
I couldn’t find the slides for lecture 10 on the course page. Do you know if they’ll be uploaded soon?
Thanks a lot!
C-3PO

  • Pros: simple, practical, human.
  • Cons: better avoided on first contact.
  • Reader’s reaction: fine, but maybe not the best first impression.

4. The “text message from the void”

A kind of teenage S.O.S.

Hi prof u got the slides 4 lecture 10? need asap

  • Pros: none.
  • Cons: all of them.
  • Reader’s reaction: confusion, then a long pause before replying.

5. The “yo prof” vibe

Yes, it exists. No, it shouldn’t.

Yo prof all good? Quick thing: when r u posting the slides for lecture 10? Btw the course is 🔥 see ya in class ✌️

  • Pros: potential TikTok virality.
  • Cons: not the tone for an email to someone you’ll ask for a recommendation letter one day.
  • Reader’s reaction: shock, resignation, existential crisis.

If you want to be formal…

  • Subject: Make it say what the email is about, course included: “Econometrics: slides for lecture 10”, not “Question” (and never empty).
  • Greeting: “Hi Prof” isn’t formal. It’s the email version of a shrug. Go with “Dear Professor Lecter”: title and surname.
  • Content: Introduce yourself (name, course) and get to the point. Avoid stuff like “I hereby write to inquire regarding…”—this isn’t a Victorian novel.
  • Before writing: Check the syllabus and the course page. Half of the answers are already there.
  • Address: Write from your university account. Emails from “xXdarklordXx@…” tend to end up in spam, or worse, get read.
  • Style: Polite, concise, and with real punctuation. And please, skip the passive-aggressive “Awaiting your reply.”
  • Timing: Write whenever you like, but send during working hours. “Schedule send” is your friend. Use it. You’ll thank yourself.

…but is all this formality always necessary?

Let’s be honest: these rules are useful, but they’re not the only way to write a good email.

You can be clear, respectful, and kind without sounding like a contract. The right tone depends on the context, your relationship with the professor, the type of university—and, let’s be honest, the country.

That’s why an email like this one:

Hi Marco,
I’m having trouble finding the slides for lecture 10. Do you know if they’ll be posted soon?
Thanks a lot, talk soon!
C-3PO

is, for me, perfectly fine. Not formal, but respectful. And at the end of the day, isn’t that what really matters?

TL;DR?

If you want to write a formal email, do it properly.
But if formality isn’t expected, there are simpler, friendlier, and still respectful alternatives.

Because, in the end, politeness beats formalism. Always.
entry.summary: Writing an email to a professor can make you question every grammatical rule and life choice you’ve ever made. Real (and tragic) examples, practical tips, and one key principle: politeness always beats empty formalism.
